averroes: Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an Andalusian Muslim philosopher, physician, and jurist, celebrated as the greatest medieval commentator on Aristotle. He defended the harmony of reason and revealed religion, arguing they are two paths to the same truth, and wrote on fate and divine foreknowledge while preserving genuine human choice.
avicenna: Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037) was a Persian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age whose medical canon shaped Europe for centuries and whose philosophy transmitted Aristotle to the medieval world. His famous floating man thought experiment argues that the soul is aware of itself independently of the body, anticipating later mind–body dualism.
benatar: David Benatar is a contemporary South African philosopher at the University of Cape Town, best known for anti-natalism: the provocative argument that coming into existence is always a serious harm, so it is wrong to create new people. He is a leading voice in contemporary philosophical pessimism.
byung-chul-han: Byung-Chul Han is a South Korean-born German philosopher known for short, sharp diagnoses of digital life. He argues that the disciplinary society Foucault described, built on surveillance and prohibition, has given way to an achievement society where people exploit and monitor themselves voluntarily.
derrick-bell: Derrick Bell was an American legal scholar and civil rights lawyer, the first Black professor tenured at Harvard Law School, and a founding figure of Critical Race Theory. He argued that racial equality advances only when it converges with white interests, and his work laid the groundwork for later intersectional analysis of race and law.
fichte: Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814) was a German philosopher who bridged Kant and Hegel, founding his own system on the self-positing I. He held that the self actively constitutes itself and its world, making freedom, self-creation, and the moral vocation of the individual central themes later echoed in existentialism.
firestone: Shulamith Firestone (1945–2012) was an American radical feminist whose book The Dialectic of Sex (1970) applied Marxist historical materialism to gender, locating the root of women's oppression in biological reproduction itself and calling for technology to free women from it. She was a central figure of second-wave feminism.
fricker: Miranda Fricker (b. 1966) is a British philosopher who coined the term epistemic injustice: the wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower, whether by having their testimony discounted or by lacking the shared concepts to make sense of their own experience. Her 2007 book made her a leading figure in social epistemology.
friedan: Betty Friedan (1921–2006) was an American writer whose The Feminine Mystique (1963) named the problem that has no name: the quiet desperation of educated 1950s housewives confined to domesticity. A co-founder of the National Organization for Women, she helped ignite second-wave feminism.
gadamer: Hans-Georg Gadamer (1900–2002) was a German philosopher, a student of Heidegger, whose Truth and Method (1960) founded philosophical hermeneutics. He argued that all understanding is historical interpretation shaped by tradition and prejudice in the neutral sense, and that understanding happens as a fusion of horizons between interpreter and text.
gramsci: Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937) was an Italian Marxist theorist who founded the Italian Communist Party and was imprisoned by Mussolini, writing his Prison Notebooks from cell. His concept of cultural hegemony explains how ruling classes dominate through consent and everyday culture rather than force alone, an idea hugely influential in cultural studies.
guy-debord: Guy Debord was a French Marxist theorist and filmmaker who led the Situationist International. In The Society of the Spectacle (1967) he argued that modern life has become mediated by images: social relations are replaced by the representation of commodities, a critique that influenced the 1968 Paris protests.
hierocles: Hierocles was an ancient Stoic philosopher, probably of the second century AD, known only from surviving fragments. His image of concentric circles of concern holds that we should progressively draw distant strangers inward, treating them more like family, one of antiquity's clearest arguments for cosmopolitan concern.
jameson: Fredric Jameson is an American Marxist literary critic, one of the most influential theorists of postmodernism. He famously analyzed postmodern culture as the cultural logic of late capitalism, connecting pastiche and the waning of historicity to the economic transformations of the contemporary world.
jung: Carl Jung (1875–1961) was a Swiss psychiatrist and founder of analytical psychology who broke with Freud. He proposed the collective unconscious, a shared psychic inheritance expressed in universal archetypes, and described the Shadow: the repressed, disowned side of the personality that must be confronted for wholeness.
korsgaard: Christine Korsgaard (b. 1952) is an American philosopher at Harvard and one of the leading Kantian ethicists working today. Her Kantian constructivism holds that moral norms are not discovered in the world but generated by our own capacity to choose our ends, grounding the Kantian idea that humanity must be treated as an end in itself.
maimonides: Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon, 1138–1204) was a medieval Jewish philosopher, rabbi, and physician, the towering intellectual figure of medieval Judaism. In his Guide for the Perplexed he sought to reconcile Aristotelian reason with Hebrew scripture, arguing that God can be described only through what God is not.
mencius: Mencius (Mengzi, 372–289 BC) was the great Confucian sage of classical China, second only to Confucius himself in the tradition's esteem. He argued that human nature is innately good, pointing to our spontaneous compassion for a child about to fall into a well, and taught that rulers who brutalize the people forfeit their legitimacy.
plumwood: Val Plumwood (1939–2008) was an Australian ecofeminist philosopher who attacked anthropocentrism and the paired dualisms, such as reason over nature and human over animal, that she saw underlying both environmental destruction and the domination of women. Her work helped found ecofeminism and modern environmental ethics.
sandel: Michael Sandel (b. 1953) is an American political philosopher at Harvard, famous for his open Justice course and books such as What Money Can't Buy. A leading communitarian, he criticizes liberal individualism for imagining an unencumbered self detached from community, history, and shared goods.
shankara: Shankara (c. 700–750 AD) was an Indian philosopher who systematized Advaita Vedanta, the nondualist school of Hindu thought. He taught that only Brahman, ultimate reality, truly exists, and that the innermost self, Atman, is identical with it, the everyday world of multiplicity being appearance shaped by maya.
umberto-eco: Umberto Eco was an Italian medievalist, semiotician, and novelist, best known for The Name of the Rose. His scholarly work examined signs, interpretation, and the limits of how far texts can mean, and in his essays he analyzed mass culture, spectacle, and the recurring features of fascist movements.
wolf: Susan Wolf (b. 1952) is an American philosopher working on ethics and the meaning of life. She argues that meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness, loving something genuinely worth loving, and her essay Moral Saints provocatively suggests that a life dominated by moral perfection would be impoverished.
xunzi: Xunzi (c. 310–235 BC) was a Confucian philosopher of classical China and Mencius's great rival on human nature. He held that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, so that goodness must be deliberately constructed through ritual, education, and cultivation rather than drawn from innate compassion.
